contributions.text_english: Diolch, Lywydd. First Minister, I want to raise a deeply disturbing case from our capital city. In March this year, 29-year-old Mohammed Abbas arrived in Britain on a small boat from France. By June, he was in custody facing criminal charges. In July, he was convicted of offences including assaulting a police officer and sentenced to 300 hours of community service. He was subsequently placed in Home Office-funded accommodation in Cardiff. Just two days later, at 2 o'clock in the morning, he entered a family home and committed sexual offences in the presence of two young girls, both under the age of 16. He has since pleaded guilty to four further offences and is awaiting sentencing. Those two young girls should have been safe in their own home. First Minister, what discussions have you had with the Home Office about this case? What assurances have you sought about the safeguarding of communities hosting asylum accommodation? And will you now commission an urgent review of the arrangements between Welsh public services and the Home Office to ensure that a case like this is never repeated?

contributions.text_english:
Holding you to account is our responsibility as an effective opposition. Take the NHS. You're promising up to 10 surgical hubs, more diagnostic capacity, stronger clinical pathways and up to 100 more general practitioners. Those are ambitious commitments and people will expect this Government to deliver them. So, my first question is this: by the end of this Senedd term, how much lower should the overall waiting lists be, when will those surgical hubs be operating at full capacity and how many additional patients will they treat? Give us the baseline. Give us the target. Give us the date. Then, this Senedd can hold you to it. 

The same applies to education. Your programme says that raising literacy and numeracy is one of the most urgent challenges facing our schools. I would agree. It also accepts the problems around persistent absence, behaviour and the pressure on the additional learning needs system. I welcome the fact that the Government recognises those problems, but recognition is the easy part. Schools cannot employ additional support with warm words, and local authorities cannot satisfy the growing demand for support with another review.

So, my second question is this: what improvement in attendance, literacy and numeracy should we expect to see by 2030, and what additional resource will actually reach the schools and councils to make the ALN system sustainable? Again, put the numbers against it. Parents and teachers need to know what success looks like. We on these opposition benches need to know what your idea of success looks like.

There is a much clearer political difference between us on the economy. This Government wants new agencies, commissions and programmes. Reform went into the election offering a different approach. We want lower taxes, better roads, stronger infrastructure and a Government that makes it easier for businesses to invest and grow here in Cymru. Your programme talks about productivity and good jobs. Fine. Productivity can be measured. Pay can be measured. Economic inactivity can be measured. Business creation can be measured. So, my third question is this: which economic measure does the First Minister want us to judge him by in 2030, and what target is he setting himself? Because if the answer is that Wales will be more prosperous, that is not enough. We need to know what progress looks like in hard figures.

I will now move on to the areas on which Reform fundamentally disagrees. First Minister, your Government remains committed to a pathway to net zero by 2040. Reform does not support that devolved target. We put greater weight on affordability, energy security and nuclear power, including the economic opportunity through small modular reactors at Wylfa in north Wales, which did not feature at all in Plaid Cymru's election manifesto. In fact, there's not much talk of north Wales at all in your programme for government, which is extremely disappointing.

On farming, you intend to continue and refine the sustainable farming scheme. We campaigned for much more substantial reform, with food production taking precedence and bureaucracy taking a back seat, rather than form filling and farming by calendar, which risks driving livestock numbers down in Wales. Those are fair and genuine differences, and people can judge the outcomes for themselves.

I also want to address the constitutional section of this programme, because it goes well beyond asking Westminster for a fair funding settlement. You are establishing a new national commission for Wales. You want justice and policing devolved, welfare devolved, further powers over energy, broadcasting, water and the Crown Estate. And Government is formally asking for the power to determine the timing, question and process of an independence referendum. Plaid Cymru is entitled to argue for those things. Reform is equally entitled to oppose them. I will never accept the notion that you have to support independence and constitutional chaos to prove you believe in Wales.

First Minister, I'm interested in what works, not what fits an ideology. Being Welsh does not require supporting independence, and standing up for Wales does not require wanting to leave the United Kingdom. So, my fourth question is this: how much public money and civil service resource will be committed to this constitutional programme during this Senedd term, and what practical outcome will you use to show that the expenditure has improved people's day-to-day lives?

Your own well-being statement says that the programme for government will be reviewed every year, and that progress will be reported annually. Good. And those reports must contain enough hard information for this Senedd and the public to judge whether you are delivering. By 2030, will people be waiting less time for treatment? Will children be attending school more regularly and achieving better results? Will wages and productivity be higher? Will businesses have confidence and invest in Wales? Will Welsh farmers be unshackled from burdensome red tape and incentivised to increase food production? I'm asking you to tell us what success looks like in numbers and time frames. Set the measures now, publish them every year, and then we will see whether this Government delivers what it has promised. Diolch yn fawr.

contributions.text_english:
You say that the education system has lacked

'clarity, coherence and direction, and literacy and numeracy have been lost in the noise of significant reform.'

So, parents will quite reasonably ask how we were ever allowed to reach that point in the first place. The latest PISA results show Wales scoring 476 in science, 459 in reading and 456 in mathematics. Welsh learners are behind the other UK nations across all three subjects, as we know. On the headline scores, Wales is now closer to Vietnam than to England in both mathematics and science. Gweinidog, I believe we should recognise this for exactly what it is: it’s a national emergency in Welsh education.

I agree, we do need clearer expectations about what children should know and when, earlier identification of those falling behind, a stronger focus on phonics and better use of assessment data. These are all very sensible suggestions. But you've said today that the national indicators will be driven by clear targets, so I would like to ask, what are those targets? What measurable improvement do you expect to see by when, and will those targets be published so that parents, teachers, this Senedd, can judge whether this plan has actually worked? Because saying that standards must improve is not the same as setting out what success looks like.

I also want to understand what this plan means for teachers on the front line of an education system in distress. You're proposing a new baseline assessment, a year 6 indicator, national indicators and greater target setting. You and I both know that teachers are under enormous pressure. I've raised before that retaining good teachers is every bit as important as recruiting them. So, what additional time, training and resources will schools receive to deliver this plan? And importantly, Minister, what are you taking away? Because if every new initiative simply means more assessments, more data collection and an increase in teacher workload, then we risk adding fuel to the fire by pushing people out of the profession.

I also want to turn to additional learning needs. You acknowledge today that schools are dealing with increasingly complex needs, growing demand for specialist support and, ironically, continued funding pressure. That is exactly why Reform argued in favour of greater funding for ALN here in Wales. But the supplementary budget you published did not provide additional funding specifically for ALN. Only when securing support for that budget became critical did the Government begin making additional offers to local authorities and schools at the coalface of ALN. So, when you say today that children will be identified earlier and receive appropriate intervention, the obvious question is: intervention from whom, and paid for by what? Identifying that a child is struggling is only the first step. Schools and councils then need teaching assistants, specialist teachers, educational psychologists and appropriate provision to actually help that child. So, do you still believe it was the right decision not to direct more money towards ALN in the supplementary budget?

When the pressures you describe in today's statement are already being felt in classrooms across Wales, your Government had the opportunity to do something about it. The funding was there, arising from greater special educational needs and disability spending in England. I'd be interested to know what representations, if any, you made during the broader negotiation stages of that budget.

And finally, Minister, accountability—atebolrwydd. You say in your statement that you are hoping to see an improvement in Wales's scores in the next PISA round. I think we need something firmer than hope. The next cohort will sit PISA, as you said, in 2029, with the results published in 2030. So, will you commit today that, when those results are published, Wales will have improved on its current scores in reading, mathematics and science? That is a straightforward measure against which this Government can be judged. Parents, teachers and indeed the children themselves deserve clarity. What does success look like? When will we see it? And who will take responsibility if it's not delivered? Will it be you, Gweinidog? Diolch yn fawr iawn i chi.

The difficulty is that farmers have been hearing that ambition for a very long time, yet, if you speak to them today, the majority don't feel like we're getting any closer to the long-term goal of eradicating the disease. Farmers still live with the same uncertainty, the same movement restrictions and the same crippling anxiety every time a test comes around. They still see healthy, productive cattle being slaughtered. I can't put into words just how distressing it is for me to read the latest data. Over 10,000 cattle were slaughtered in Wales last year alone, with 479 new herd incidents detected—479. My heart goes out to every person doing their best to cope with the mental strain caused by bovine TB. That is why Reform has brought this debate forward today, because we don't think it's good enough to simply carry on with the same conversation we've been having for years and expect farmers to believe that something is about to change.

One thing that has struck me over the last few weeks, and, indeed, during the election campaign, is that I've listened to Plaid Cymru say that they will follow the science. I don't disagree with that. In fact, that's exactly what the Government should be doing. But I keep coming back to the same question: follow the science to where? This isn't a new disease. We're not starting from scratch. Welsh Governments have had years of evidence available to them. They've had scientific advice. They've had the technical advisory group. They've had veterinary expertise, years of surveillance data and years of lived experience from the farmers themselves. Farmers in my constituency aren't asking whether the Government has enough evidence yet. They're asking what the Government has actually concluded from the scientific evidence it already has. Evidence doesn't make decisions; Ministers do. And this current Minister has years of experience in opposition. He knows better than anyone exactly what the science is telling him. At some point, this Government has to demonstrate what it has learned from the evidence it has spent years collecting, and that it's ready to harness that data and take meaningful, tangible steps to manage bovine TB in Wales.

I find myself thinking back to what Plaid Cymru used to say when they sat on the opposition benches. Llyr Gruffydd spoke passionately about bovine TB, he challenged Labour's approach, he spoke about the pressure on farming families and questioned whether the existing strategy was delivering what farmers had been promised. He spoke about the need to listen to the evidence and to the industry. Those were perfectly legitimate questions to ask and they're just as legitimate now that Plaid Cymru is in Government.

Farmers don’t see politics in the way we do. They don’t look at which benches people are sitting on; they simply want to know whether anything is going to actually change. What is this Senedd doing to help them, to make their lives easier and to give the next generation of farmers a future? If the answer is that we need more time, I suspect many farmers will say they've already given successive Governments enough time. If the answer is another review, they'll say that we've had reviews before. If the answer is more evidence, they'll quite reasonably ask what happened to all the evidence that we've already gathered. That isn't an argument against science—quite the opposite; it's an argument for having the confidence to act on the science.

I've never accepted that this debate should be reduced to people choosing sides before they've even discussed the evidence. Whether it's cattle controls, biosecurity, vaccination or a controlled wildlife cull, surely the starting point has to be an honest assessment of what is and isn't working. Because if we can't ask those questions now, after everything farmers have lived through, when can we?

The uncomfortable reality is that, after decades of increasingly stringent cattle controls, Wales is still recording thousands of reactor cattle every year and hundreds of new herd incidents. It is entirely reasonable to ask whether the strategy, taken as a whole, is getting us where we all want to be. I don't think that it's a criticism of farmers—quite the opposite; farmers have done what successive Governments have asked of them. They have accepted tighter controls, greater costs and more bureaucracy, because they believed they were contributing towards better management of the disease. Government now has to show the same willingness to examine its own approach, because—[Interruption.] No, I'd like to make progress. Behind every statistic is a family trying to make a living; behind every breakdown are years of breeding, investment and hard work. I don't believe farmers expect miracles, they know that this is one of the most difficult animal health challenges we face, but they do expect leadership, especially when the Minister talked such a good game in opposition.

With all due respect—and I say this as constructively as possible—does the Minister want his legacy in Government to be that of a doer, or does he want to be remembered as a talker or a promiser? Talk is cheap, farmers are clear: they don't want hope, they want action. Diolch yn fawr.

contributions.item_title_en: 7. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Skills and Tertiary Education: Priorities for Skills and Tertiary Education
contributions.text_english:
I'd like to thank the Deputy Minister for his statement, and I'd also like to declare an interest, in that I worked in the education sector myself until Easter this year. I don't think anyone in the Siambr would disagree that Wales needs a stronger skills system, and if we're serious about growing our economy, attracting investment and giving young people a reason to build their future here, then skills have to sit right at the heart of that. And there's plenty in your statement that I welcome, particularly about the Welsh language and being able to broaden the use of that in the sector, also a proper look at the skills Wales is going to need in the future is sensible, and, of course, employers should have a much stronger voice in shaping what is taught and where public money is spent.

But, Deputy Minister, I couldn't help feeling that this statement contained a great deal about how Government intends to think about these challenges and much less about what is actually going to change. We have a skills audit, we have a future skills summit, we have a national strategy to come, we have reviews, consultations and engagement. My concern is that businesses across Wales don't feel they have the luxury of waiting for another round of policy development; they're trying to recruit today.

One thing I was particularly pleased to hear was your commitment to making sure the skills system supports Wales's wider economic ambitions. If that genuinely is the Government's ambition, then surely we need to start preparing now for the opportunities we already know could be on the horizon. Take Wylfa in my constituency, for example. Whether it's new nuclear or small modular reactors, if those projects move forward, they'll require thousands of skilled people—not just engineers, but welders, electricians, project managers, construction workers, technicians and apprentices. Those skills cannot be created overnight. By the time a final investment decision is made, the training pipeline should already be in place.

Can the Deputy Minister therefore tell us whether Medr, our further education colleges and apprenticeship providers have already been asked to begin planning for these opportunities? Because if we're waiting until the contracts are signed before we start training people, we're already behind. The same principle applies more broadly: businesses don't just want to be consulted, they want to know the Government is prepared to respond when they identify genuine skills shortages.

So, if this audit comes back and tells you what employers have been saying for years, that we don't have enough people coming through into engineering, construction, manufacturing or digital industries, what will the Government actually do differently? How quickly will funding follow the evidence and how will success be measured? Because, Deputy Minister, I don't think employers will judge this work on the number of strategies that are published; they'll judge it on whether it's any easier to recruit the people they need. Young people won't judge it on how many summits have taken place; they'll judge it on whether the qualifications they're studying lead to secure, well-paid jobs here in Wales. And communities like mine in north Wales will judge it on whether major investment creates opportunities for local people or whether those jobs end up being filled from elsewhere because we didn't prepare in time.

I genuinely hope this work succeeds, because Wales cannot afford another decade of talking about skills while other parts of the UK get on with delivering them. Now is the time to make sure our education and skills system is preparing people not just for the jobs we have today, but for the industries we want Wales to lead tomorrow. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

contributions.item_title_en: 4. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language: Welsh Language Priorities
contributions.text_english:
May I also thank the Minister for her statement on the Welsh language today? There is so much that we can all agree on in this statement, so thank you very much for that. Some of my story: as someone who grew up in a non-Welsh speaking home but learned Welsh at school, you won't find anyone who feels more passionately than me in favour of the language. My parents decided to send me to a Welsh-medium primary school and then a bilingual secondary school. And looking back, that was one of the most precious gifts that they could have given me. And there is a family story that explains why this is such a personal issue for me. My grandfather, Silgwyn Weston, was a miner in south Wales. He didn't speak a word of English until he was around eight years old, but having received advice from his sister after she moved to university in London, he decided that the best way of providing the greatest opportunities to his children was to speak English at home. As a result, my mother lost her Welsh. And the truth is that I wouldn’t have had the opportunity to speak Welsh at all if my parents hadn’t opted for Welsh-medium education for me. 

That meant that there was something very special between myself and my grandfather. We were the only two members of the family who could hold a natural conversation in Welsh. Silgwyn Weston was a very proud Welshman. And in his final years, there was one constant—his hearing was somehow always better if the conversation was about rugby or if someone spoke Welsh to him.

As a learner, the journey wasn’t always easy. There were times when my friends refused to speak to me in Welsh because they’d got to know me through the medium of English first. But, on the other side of things, one of my best friends admitted that her English wouldn’t have been half as good had she not been friends with me. 

That’s the beauty of bilingualism. Learning one language doesn’t mean the loss of the other. Both strengthen each other. I spent years seeking every opportunity to improve my Welsh, particularly when I was teaching in London. Understanding, reading and writing are one thing. But the final step, and the hardest step, is reaching the point where you can naturally start a conversation in Welsh without thinking twice. And, if I'm honest, not being afraid of a bit of Wenglish helps along the way. 

Today, other than the odd technical term I’m still learning, I feel very confident in my Welsh. But I also acknowledge that so much of our lives, our television programmes and our work happen in English, that learning a language is a lifelong journey. That’s why I’m proud that I have encouraged my colleagues in Reform Wales to start learning Welsh here at the Senedd. We now try to greet each other in Welsh in the office, and more and more of us are mustering the courage to use Welsh in the Chamber—as we always talk about, using a little bit of Welsh all the time. That's crucially important. So, that proves that the Welsh language doesn't have to be a party political issue.

I agree with the Minister when she said that the language is at the heart of our culture and our identity as a nation. I also welcome the fact that the Minister has made it clear that it's the Government as a whole's responsibility, not the responsibility of one Minister. If that is true, then that must be seen in all Government portfolios, not just in education. And I believe too that there is one thing that everyone in this Chamber can agree on today: the Welsh language belongs to us all, whatever your ability, your background or your politics.

But where the Government goes wrong is by suggesting that legislation, strategies and targets are the only things that will secure the future of the Welsh language. We can’t force people to love a language. We can’t legislate for enthusiasm. We can’t create Welsh-speaking communities through targets alone. The Welsh language flourishes when people choose to use it at home, in the workplace, in the pub, on the rugby pitch and on the street. I also welcome the intention to strengthen the Welsh language in digital and AI. If the Welsh language isn't available in those technologies, then there is a risk that it will be left behind.

We must ensure that the Welsh language is never used as a political weapon. The Welsh language belongs to us all, as we've already mentioned. But we must also ensure that the desire to strengthen the Welsh language doesn't draw lines between communities. The Welsh language belongs to all communities in Wales, and all communities deserve the same support in using and developing the language.

So, I'd like to ask the three questions of the Minister. First, the Minister said that the Welsh language is the responsibility of the whole Cabinet: what arrangements will be in place to ensure that every Minister is accountable for delivering that? Secondly, how will the Government measure an increase in the daily use of the language, rather than focusing on simply the number of speakers? And finally, what practical steps will be taken to help learners to use the Welsh language naturally in their communities once they have left school or completed courses?

You can't force people to love a language. It starts with opportunity, it grows with confidence and it prospers when people feel welcome to use the language. The Welsh language belongs to the people of Wales. It belongs to all of us. Thank you.

Gaf i ddiolch i'r Gweinidog am ei datganiad ar yr iaith Gymraeg heddiw? Mae yna gymaint y medrwn ni i gyd gytuno arno fo yn y datganiad hwnnw, so diolch yn fawr am hwnna. Tipyn o stori amdanaf i, felly: fel rhywun a dyfodd i fyny mewn cartref di-Gymraeg ac wedi dysgu'r Gymraeg yn yr ysgol, mi fyddai'n anodd ichi ffeindio unrhyw un sy'n fwy angerddol na fi dros yr iaith bellach. Penderfynodd fy rhieni i fy anfon i ysgol gynradd Gymraeg a wedyn i ysgol uwchradd ddwyieithog. Wrth edrych yn ôl, dyna oedd un o'r rhoddion mwyaf gwerthfawr y gallan nhw wedi ei roi i fi. Ac mae yna stori deuluol sy'n egluro ba mor bersonol mae hwn i fi. Roedd fy nhaid, Silgwyn Weston, yn löwr yn ne Cymru. Nid oedd yn siarad gair o Saesneg nes oedd o tua wyth oed, ond ar ôl cael cyngor gan ei chwaer ar ôl iddi hi symud i Lundain i'r brifysgol, penderfynodd mai'r ffordd orau o roi'r cyfleoedd gorau i'w blant oedd siarad Saesneg gartref. O ganlyniad, collodd fy mam y Gymraeg. A'r gwir yw na fyddwn innau wedi cael y Gymraeg o gwbl oni bai bod fy rhieni wedi dewis addysg Gymraeg i mi.

Roedd hynny'n golygu bod rhywbeth arbennig iawn rhyngof i a'm taid. Ni oedd yr unig ddau yn y teulu oedd yn gallu cynnal sgwrs naturiol drwy'r Gymraeg. Cymro balch iawn oedd Silgwyn Weston. Ac yn ei flynyddoedd olaf roedd un peth wastad yn wir—roedd ei glyw rywsut yn llawer gwell os oedd y sgwrs am rygbi neu os oedd rhywun yn siarad Cymraeg efo fo.

Fel dysgwr, doedd y daith ddim yn hawdd bob amser. Roedd adegau pan oedd fy ffrindiau i'n gwrthod siarad Cymraeg hefo fi gan eu bod nhw wedi dod i'm hadnabod i drwy'r Saesneg yn gyntaf. Ond, ar yr ochr arall, cyfaddefodd un o'm ffrindiau gorau wrthyf na fyddai ei Saesneg hi hanner cystal oni bai ei bod hi'n ffrindiau efo fi.

Dyna harddwch dwyieithrwydd. Nid yw dysgu un iaith yn golygu colli'r llall. Mae'r ddwy yn cryfhau ei gilydd. Treuliais flynyddoedd yn chwilio am bob cyfle i wella fy Nghymraeg, yn enwedig pan oeddwn i'n dysgu yn Llundain. Mae deall, darllen ac ysgrifennu yn un peth. Ond y cam olaf, a'r cam anoddaf, yw cyrraedd y pwynt lle rydych chi'n gallu dechrau sgwrs yn y Gymraeg yn naturiol, heb feddwl dwywaith. Ac, os dwi'n onest, mae peidio â bod ofn tipyn bach o Wenglish yn helpu ar hyd y ffordd.

Heddiw, heblaw am ambell derm technegol rwy'n dal i ddysgu, rwy'n hyderus iawn yn fy Nghymraeg. Ond rwy'n cydnabod hefyd, gan fod cymaint o'n bywydau, ein teledu a'n gwaith yn digwydd drwy gyfrwng y Saesneg, fod dysgu iaith yn daith sy'n parhau drwy gydol oes. Dyna pam dwi'n falch fy mod i wedi annog fy nghydweithwyr yn Reform Cymru i ddechrau dysgu Cymraeg yma yn y Senedd. Bellach rydym yn trio cyfarch ein gilydd yn y swyddfa drwy'r Gymraeg, ac mae mwy a mwy ohonom yn magu'r hyder i ddefnyddio'r Gymraeg yn y Siambr—fel rydym ni'n sôn, defnyddio darnau bach o'r Gymraeg trwy'r adeg. Mae hynna'n hollbwysig. So, mae hynny'n profi nad oes rhaid i'r Gymraeg fod yn fater pleidiol.

Dwi'n cytuno â'r Gweinidog pan ddywedodd hi fod yr iaith yn ganolog i'n diwylliant a'n hunaniaeth fel cenedl. Rwy'n croesawu hefyd y ffaith bod y Gweinidog wedi dweud yn glir mai cyfrifoldeb y Llywodraeth gyfan yw'r Gymraeg, nid dim ond un Gweinidog. Os yw hynny'n wir, mae'n rhaid i'r egwyddor honna gael ei gweld ym mhob portffolio Llywodraeth Cymru, nid dim ond ym maes addysg. A dwi'n credu hefyd fod un peth y gall pawb yn y Siambr hon gytuno arno heddiw: mae'r Gymraeg i bawb, waeth beth ydy lefel eich gallu, eich cefndir neu eich gwleidyddiaeth.

Ond lle mae'r Llywodraeth yn mynd o'i le yw pan fo hi'n awgrymu mai deddfwriaeth, strategaethau a thargedau yn unig fydd yn sicrhau dyfodol yr iaith. Ni allwn orfodi pobl i garu iaith. Ni allwn ddeddfu brwdfrydedd. Ni allwn greu cymunedau Cymraeg drwy dargedau yn unig. Mae'r Gymraeg yn ffynnu pan fydd pobl yn dewis ei defnyddio yn y cartref, yn y gweithle, yn y dafarn, ar y cae rygbi ac ar y stryd. Croesawaf hefyd y bwriad i gryfhau'r Gymraeg yn y byd digidol ac AI. Os nad yw'r Gymraeg yn bresennol yn y technolegau hynna, mae perygl bydd hi'n cael ei gadael ar ôl.

Mae'n rhaid i ni sicrhau nad yw'r Gymraeg byth yn cael ei defnyddio fel arf gwleidyddol. Mae'r Gymraeg yn perthyn i bawb, fel rydym ni'n sôn. Ond mae'n rhaid inni hefyd sicrhau nad yw'r awydd i gryfhau'r Gymraeg yn troi'n ymarfer o dynnu llinellau rhwng cymunedau. Mae'r Gymraeg yn perthyn i bob rhan o Gymru ac mae pob cymuned yn haeddu'r un gefnogaeth i'w defnyddio a'i datblygu.

Felly, hoffwn ofyn tri chwestiwn i'r Gweinidog. Yn gyntaf, dywedodd y Gweinidog mai cyfrifoldeb y Cabinet cyfan yw'r Gymraeg: pa drefniadau fydd ar waith i sicrhau bod pob Gweinidog yn atebol am gyflawni hynny? contributions.item_title_en: 5. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language: Priorities for Education
contributions.text_english:
What concerns me ever so slightly about the statement is while there's been a lot of emphasis on recruitment, there's not quite enough detail when it comes to retention. What precisely is the Welsh Government going to do to retain the teaching workforce we already have? Cabinet Minister, you acknowledged in your statement today that too many educators leave the profession too early and that we need to keep them in the classroom. On that point, I agree, but the question is: how? What specifically is going to change for teachers working in our schools?

Having been a teacher myself, I understand why many are leaving the profession. Despite successive recruitment drives, Wales continues to struggle with teacher retention. We're losing experienced teachers faster than we can replace them. That concern is only amplified by our shared ambitions for bilingual and Welsh-medium education. The challenge is not simply finding teachers; it's finding teachers with the language skills needed to deliver those ambitions. Every experienced bilingual teacher who leaves the profession is not easily replaced. If we're already struggling to retain the workforce we have today, how can the Government realistically hope to deliver the workforce it will need tomorrow?

Cabinet Minister, you say that you want to address issues associated with workload, but I would like to know, and I think teachers would like to know, what exactly that means. Where are the tangible changes our current teachers can expect to see? So far, there's been very little detail about what workload reduction would look like in practice. Thinking of the secondary sector, for example, would there be time off timetables to mark mock exams and controlled assessments?

More notably, there was very little mention of what has undoubtedly become one of the biggest problems facing education, and that is the deterioration of pupil behaviour in schools. Cabinet Secretary, where is the confidence and determination to get to grips with the rise of violence in schools? A recent Welsh teaching union survey found that 43 per cent of teachers had been shoved or barged by pupils, 12 per cent had been hit or punched, 9 per cent had been kicked, and 3 per cent reported being headbutted. Almost half—and this is particularly distressing—said that they felt blamed when raising those concerns about poor behaviour. Behaviour is now one of the biggest barriers to teacher retention, yet today's statement has remarkably little to say about it. A teacher in my constituency, for example, recently said, 'For the first time in my 25-year career, I don't feel safe in school'.

I really don't think today's statement will have instilled much confidence in our teaching workforce that the Welsh Government intends to get to grips with violent behaviour or unsustainable workloads. And if it can't get to grips with those two things, we will continue to lose our teachers. Cabinet Secretary, in your statement today, you also said the education system is currently failing too many of our children and young people, and on that point, I absolutely agree. But what I find slightly extraordinary is that Plaid Cymru now seems to be talking about the state of Welsh education, as though they spent the last 26 years glued to the opposition benches. Plaid Cymru has spent years helping Labour govern Wales, shaping budgets, legislation and education policy.

Indeed, Plaid Members are often keen to remind us of the achievements delivered through their agreements with Labour, whether that's free school meals, childcare expansion or other policies. They're more than happy to stand up and claim the credit for those successes. But Plaid Cymru can't have it both ways. If they want to claim credit for the successes of working with Labour, they must also accept responsibility for the failures. They cannot claim ownership of free school meals one minute, then pretend to be an innocent bystander when educational standards fall short the next, because teachers, parents and pupils don't care which party gets the credit. They care about outcomes. And after more than two decades of Labour Government, supported at various times by Plaid Cymru, those outcomes simply aren't good enough.

So, I end by asking this: can you reassure this Senedd that you are speaking directly to teachers and teaching unions about how exactly your Government will improve teacher working conditions? Because the reality is that recruitment alone will not solve this problem. A change of culture is needed. You can recruit all the new teachers you like, but if your experienced teachers continue leaving the profession, Welsh education will simply be running to stand still. Every one of us here can remember a teacher who changed our lives. The problem is that experience takes years to build, but only a moment to lose. If this Government fails to address workload and behaviour in detail, Wales will continue to lose our best teachers, and when teachers leave, it is not the Ministers who pay the price, it is our children. Diolch yn fawr.

contributions.text_english: Minister, thank you very much for your statement. I suspect that everyone in this Chamber would agree that reducing child poverty and helping families with the cost of living in Wales are very important objectives.

contributions.item_title_en: 4. Statement by the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice and Equality: Priorities for Social Justice and Equality
contributions.text_english:
It's actually a refreshing change to hear Wales being prioritised, given your commitment to overseas spending, such as planting trees in foreign countries and pointless vanity offices in Brussels and Beijing. Every child deserves the best possible start in life, and affordable childcare can play an important role in helping parents into work.

However, having listened carefully to your statement, I was struck by what was missing. You spoke of respect, solidarity and fairness. You spoke of transformational change. You spoke of expert groups, planning, testing and future phases of expansion. But what families across Wales need today is clarity. Your manifesto promised what you describe as the most generous childcare offer anywhere in the United Kingdom. That is a significant commitment. Yet, today, we have heard very little about how much this policy will cost, where the funding will come from or when parents can realistically expect it to be delivered. The Welsh public are entitled to know the answers to those questions. We are all aware of the financial pressures facing Wales. Local authorities are under strain, the NHS remains under enormous pressure, schools are facing difficult budget decisions, businesses continue to struggle with rising costs. Against that backdrop, it's entirely reasonable to ask how a universal childcare offer of this scale will be funded.

Minister, your manifesto was presented to voters as a fully costed programme for government. If that is the case, surely the Government already knows the total cost of this policy, surely it already knows where the money will come from, and surely it already has a road map for delivery. Yet today's statement appears to suggest that many of those details are still being worked through by a newly established expert steering group. 

So, I would be grateful if you could provide some clarity. Can you tell the Senedd today what the estimated total cost of delivering this childcare offer will be? Can you explain which budgets or funding streams will be used to pay for it? And can you set out a clear timetable for delivery so that parents, childcare providers and local authorities know exactly what to expect and when?
